newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin lectures allies on "realities".
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin lectures allies on "realities".

text.p: Prime Minister Lionel Jospin lectured members of France's new leftist parliamentary majority on Tuesday on the need for discipline following an uproar over the closing of Renault's car assembly plant in Belgium.

The Socialist-led government's powers in trying to prevent the Vilvoorde plant from closing were "extremely limited", spokesman Manuel Valls quoted Jospin as telling the National Assembly's Socialist group behind closed doors.

"In such circumstances, he hoped Socialist officials would not want to put responsibility (for the plant's closure) on the government's shoulders, particularly since this might encourage other majority partners to raise their voices on this type of issue," Valls told reporters.
Socialist deputies later said they had voted to endorse the government's action on the Renault matter.
Communist Party leader Robert Hue said the plant's closure would not threaten his party's participation in Jospin's cabinet, which has three Communists.
"We do not hesitate to say that we are unhappy with what was done with Vilvoorde but there is no questioning the Communist participation in the government," Hue told reporters.
"Once the debate is over and the decisions taken, we will stick together," Jean-Marc Ayrault, president of the National Assembly's Socialist group, said after the meeting with Jospin.

Communist members of Jospin's month-old leftist majority, an alliance of Socialists, Communists and Greens, complained loudly at the weekend when Renault affirmed an earlier decision to close down the plant despite the new government's campaign promise to seek alternatives.

Leading Socialist Henri Emmanuelli, head of the Assembly's finance committee, joined the chorus, saying Renault had not seriously considered reducing the working week to save jobs and complaining the carmaker's plans would boost state expenses.
Jospin, who is to give on Thursday at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) his first live television interview since taking power, told the Socialist MPs he felt he had kept his campaign pledge.

He said that as a result of the government review of the Vilvoorde issue after the left took power, the 2,900 workers still at the factory would benefit from better settlement terms and a promise of no outright layoffs.
"There are promises, and there is the will to keep them, but there are also the economic and social realities of the nation," Jospin told the deputies, according to Valls.

Conservative President Jacques Chirac, meanwhile, said on Tuesday that structural reforms were required for the French economy to adapt to global markets but that all citizens must share equally in the burden of change.

"Globalisation and its accompanying -- and often painful -- changes, reconversions and restructurings, require considerable adaptation on the part of all of our fellow citizens," Chirac told a journalists' association.
"The modernisation of France, which is undeniably a necessity, can only be undertaken...if we pursue together the path of a modern and responsible solidarity," he said.
He said social welfare benefits, pension plans and family aid programmes would have to be adapted "to respond to our new needs".

He said social responsibility under the European model could only be undertaken in unison with all of France's European partners and hailed Britain's acceptance of a social chapter in an updated Maastricht treaty on European integration at a European Union summit last month in Amsterdam.
